newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japan to get WTO wish list despite low profile.
newsitem.headline: Japan to get WTO wish list despite low profile.

text.p: Japan's trade minister failed to appear at all and its top diplomat stayed just two days, but Tokyo still looked set to score its main points at this week's gathering of a pivotal world trade organisation.

Long a loud cheerleader for the world free trade system, Tokyo suffered a major embarrassment when its trade minister had to stay home from the World Trade Organisation's (WTO) first ministerial meeting due to a scandal at his ministry.

Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, originally set to make only a one-day appearance on Tuesday, extended his stay until Wednesday evening in an apparent effort to erase any impression that Tokyo might be giving free trade short shrift.

But although Japan often appeared left in the shadows while tough-talking trade chiefs from the United States and Europe stole the limelight, its negotiators looked set on Thursday to come away with much of what they had sought.

The conference, ending on Friday, will be capped by the announcement of a ministerial declaration reaffirming WTO members' commitment to free trade and setting the world trade watchdog's agenda into the 21st century.

"Of course there were negotiations that only the minister could take part in, but at other levels trade bureaucrats and officials from other ministries were doing their jobs," said an executive from giant electronics firm Mitsubishi Electric Corp.
"I don't think Japan's bargaining power was weakened by the absence of the trade minister," he added.
High on Tokyo's wish list was an agreement to scrap tariffs in the fast-growing and lucrative global information technology markets, where its corporations are major players.
Washington led the initiative for the Information Technology Agreement (ITA) and was strongly backed by Tokyo.

After days of intense talks, European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan announced on Thursday that the EU and the United States had ironed out their differences over ITA, which would eliminate infotech tariffs in stages by 2000.

Compromise between the United States and the EU had resulted in a deal covering the bulk of industrial information technology products, as well as digital photocopiers and capacitors -- circuits used in electronic equipment-- while excluding consumer electronics and audio materials. Final agreement depends on countries representing about 90 percent of world trade in the sector joining the pact by March 15, 1997.
A senior Japanese trade official said the Big Four trade partners -- the United States, the EU, Japan and Canada -- had settled most of their disputes over what products would be covered by the ITA.

In all, some 30 countries, including key Asia-Pacific nations, were likely to be among those initially joining the accord, details of which remain to be worked out by negotiators in Geneva next month, the official told reporters.
The infotech deal is good news for Japanese business, which is happy to see other countries' infotech tariffs fall to the zero-levels Tokyo had already pledged to implement by 1999.
"This is by all means welcome," said an executive from Mitsubishi Electric. "It is very welcome that there will now be a level playing field."

Japan also looked likely to be satisfied with an expected WTO decision to set up groups to study the issue of the treatment of foreign investment and competition policy, moves that had been opposed by developing nations loath to see the WTO expand its agenda.
"In general, things have gone the way we wanted," the Mitsubishi Electric official said.
